name: Urdu
variety: Standard Urdu, educated speech (Delhi-Lucknow norm as used in Pakistan and India); formant and duration figures come from Lahore speakers
sources: Schmidt, Ruth Laila (1999). Urdu: An Essential Grammar. London: Routledge.
Schmidt, Ruth Laila (2003). Urdu. In Cardona, George & Jain, Dhanesh (eds.), The Indo-Aryan Languages. London: Routledge.
Kachru, Yamuna (1990). Hindi-Urdu. In Comrie, Bernard (ed.), The World's Major Languages. Oxford University Press.
Ohala, Manjari (1999). Hindi. In Handbook of the International Phonetic Association, Cambridge University Press, 100-103 (same sound system).
Masica, Colin P. (1991). The Indo-Aryan Languages. Cambridge University Press.
Hussain, Sarmad (1997). Phonetic Correlates of Lexical Stress in Urdu. PhD dissertation, Northwestern University.
Fatima, Nakhat & Aden, Rabea (2003). Vowel structure of Urdu. CRULP Annual Student Report 2002-2003, Center for Research in Urdu Language Processing, Lahore.

Saleem, Abdul Mannan; Kabir, Hasan; Riaz, Muhammad Khurram; Rafique, Muhammad Mustafa; Khalid, Nauman & Shahid, Syed Raza (2002). Urdu consonantal and vocalic sounds. CRULP Annual Student Report 2001-2002, Center for Research in Urdu Language Processing, Lahore.
Lisker, Leigh & Abramson, Arthur S. (1964). A cross-language study of voicing in initial stops: acoustical measurements. Word 20(3), 384-422 (Hindi speaker).
Schertz, Jessamyn & Khan, Sameer ud Dowla (2020). Acoustic cues in production and perception of the four-way stop laryngeal contrast in Hindi and Urdu. Journal of Phonetics 81, 100979.
Kelkar, Ashok R. (1968). Studies in Hindi-Urdu I: Introduction and Word Phonology. Poona: Deccan College.
Féry, Caroline (2010). Indian languages as intonational 'phrase languages'. In Hasnain, I. & Chaudhury, S. (eds.), Festschrift to honour Ramakant Agnihotri. Delhi: Aakar.
Khan, Sameer ud Dowla (2016). The intonation of South Asian languages: towards a comparative analysis. Proceedings of Formal Approaches to South Asian Languages 6, 23-36.

vowel_formants.speaker: adult male (mean of 5 speakers, Lahore; stressed monosyllables in a b_l frame, 5 repetitions)
vowel_formants.notes: The same source gives short allophones next to /ɦ/ (F1/F2/F3): [ɛ] 547/1823/2628 (first vowel of /ʃəɦər/, 136 ms), and the very short [e] 448/1848/2448, [o] 450/1210/2311 and [ɔ] 523/1048/2528 (71-79 ms).

contrasts: four-way laryngeal contrast in stops and affricates: voiceless unaspirated, voiceless aspirated, voiced, breathy voiced
retroflex flaps /ɽ ɽʱ/ versus the tap /ɾ/ and versus retroflex stops
three short lax vowels /ɪ ə ʊ/ against seven long peripheral vowels; length goes together with quality
consonant gemination (written with tashdid, which is usually left out)
Perso-Arabic consonants /q x ɣ z f ʒ/ are part of the educated norm: /q/ : /k/, /x/ : /kʰ/, /ɣ/ : /ɡ/, /z/ : /dʒ/
allophony: /ə/ is [ɛ] next to /ɦ/ when a consonant or word boundary follows the /ɦ/ (/pəɦlaː/ [pɛɦlaː], /ʃəɦər/ [ʃɛɦɛr]); [ɔ] when /ʊ/ follows (/bəɦʊt̪/ [bɔɦɔt̪]); short [e] and [o] occur before /ɦ/ in words like /beɦt̪ər/, /ʃoɦrət̪/
/ʋ/ varies between [ʋ], [v] and [w]; [w] as an onglide after a consonant
/ɦ/ is breathy voiced between voiced sounds
breathy voiced stops have a voiced closure and a breathy release into the vowel
/n/ is homorganic before stops ([m ɳ ɲ ŋ])
/ɾ/ is a tap, trilled when geminate
the letter ain is not pronounced as a consonant; it lengthens or colours the neighbouring vowel
/q/ is replaced by [k] and /ɣ x/ by [ɡ kʰ] in less formal speech
syllable_structure: (C)(C)V(C)(C); final clusters are common in Perso-Arabic words (/vəqt̪/, /d̪oːst̪/), often broken by a short vowel in casual speech
phonotactics: schwa deletion as in Hindi; the script does not write short vowels at all, so they must be known from the word
/ɽ ɽʱ ŋ/ do not occur word-initially
geminates are medial and follow a short vowel
the letters ye and vao are ambiguous between /iː eː ɛː/ and /uː oː ɔː/ when vowel signs are left out

stress.rule: Stress falls on the heaviest syllable, in a tie on the rightmost non-final one; in practice the syllable with a long (peripheral) vowel, otherwise the first syllable (Kelkar 1968; Hussain 1997).
stress.cues: longer duration and a low pitch target on the stressed syllable followed by a rise, as reported by Hussain 1997; no vowel reduction

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none in quality; schwa is short and deleted in weak positions
rhythm.notes: The class is the usual textbook label. No nPVI value and no measurement of final lengthening could be verified.

length.notes: In stressed monosyllables long vowels last 222-244 ms and short vowels 122-136 ms for male speakers (ratio about 1.8), Fatima & Aden 2003. Geminates have roughly twice the closure of singletons.

voice_onset_time_ms.source: Lisker & Abramson 1964 (one Hindi speaker, word-initial stops; the stop system is the same, no Urdu table could be verified)

intonation.declarative: each non-final content word with its clitics forms a phrase with a rise, low on the prominent syllable and high at the right edge; the final phrase, usually the verb, is low or falling
intonation.yes_no_question: same rising phrases, final high boundary with the rise on the last syllable; the particle kyā is optional
intonation.wh_question: the wh-word before the verb carries an expanded rise, pitch is compressed after it, low boundary
intonation.continuation: high right edge on non-final phrases
intonation.accent_shape: L*...H rise per phrase: low on the stressed syllable, peak at the end of the phrase
intonation.notes: Described mostly from Hindi data (Féry 2010; Khan 2016); Hussain 1997 confirms the low target on the stressed syllable for Urdu.

phonation: breathy voiced (murmured) stops and affricates /bʱ d̪ʱ ɖʱ dʒʱ ɡʱ/ and flap /ɽʱ/
prevoicing together with aspiration noise identifies the breathy stops; breathy voice quality on the vowel can replace either cue (Schertz & Khan 2020)

problems: Breathy voiced stops are a modal voiced closure plus an added voiceless aspiration sample (inherited from the Hindi base table); no breathy voice on the vowel. IPA output writes ʰ for ʱ.
The script leaves short vowels out and eSpeak guesses them: عورت gives [aoːrət] for [ɔːrət̪], and the long vowel letters are always read as eː, oː, never ɛː, ɔː (بیٹھنا [beːʈʰnaː], چودہ [coːda]).
Nasalised vowels inside a word are written with the letter nun and are read as vowel plus [n]: چاند [caːnd], آنکھ [aːnkʰ]; also word-final in نہیں [nahiːn].
/ɽʱ/ is produced as flap + [h] + schwa: پڑھنا gives [pʌɽhənaː].
/r/ is always the trill [R], where the Hindi voice uses a tap.
Two different short central vowels are used for the same phoneme /ə/ ([a] from the zabar rules, [ʌ] or [ə] from the inherent-vowel rules): کرنا [karnaː] but پھل [pʰʌl].
Final choti he is a short [a] (کمرہ [kamra]) where speakers have a long vowel.
Intonation uses the generic eSpeak tunes; no rising phrase on each content word.
good: schwa before h plus consonant is [ɛ]: پہلا [pɛhlaː], کہنا [kɛhnaː], شہر [ʃɛhɛr]
the loan consonants q x ɣ z f ʒ are all present
a large exception list covers many common words whose vowels are not written
dental and retroflex stops and the retroflex flap are distinct

notes: The two diphthongs are not separate phonemes: [əɪ̯ əʊ̯] are realisations of /ɛː ɔː/ before /j ʋ/ and in some regional accents. Urdu and Hindi share one phonology; the differences are the firmer status of /q x ɣ z f ʒ/, the absence of /ɳ/ and /ʂ/, and the Perso-Arabic script, which hides short vowels, gemination and word-internal nasalisation.
